newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European aerospace body urges probe of Boeing/McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: European aerospace body urges probe of Boeing/McDonnell merger.

text.p: The European aerospace industry called on the European Commission Thursday to conduct a "thorough" analysis of the Boeing Co.'s planned acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp.

The European Association of Aerospace Industries, which represents the Airbus Industrie consortium and its partner companies, said the proposed $13.3 billion merger would "substantially modify the competitive situation between European and U.S. aerospace industries."
Seattle-based Boeing formally asked the European Commission this week to clear its proposed acquisition of St. Louis-based McDonnell Douglas, a commission official said Thursday.

The commission, which must review all large mergers and acquisitions that affect the European Union's market, has about a month to decide whether to clear the deal or, as is more likely, to start an in-depth probe.
The case is expected to reignite a long-standing dispute over government subsidies paid to the industry on both sides of the Atlantic.
The EU side points the finger at generously calculated defence contract prices in the United States, of which military jet maker McDonnell Douglas has been a prime beneficiary.
The AECMA said Boeing, already the world's largest manufacturer of civilian aircraft, could also benefit from those pricing practices after the merger.

"The U.S. government approach of indirect financial support to the aerospace industry through civil and military government contracts will be facilitated by a quantum jump in pooling the primary civil business of Boeing with the primary military business of McDonnell Douglas," the AECMA said.
"The merger will substantially modify the competitive situation between European and U.S. aerospace industries in particular, but not only, in the civil transport aircraft industry.
"This change comes from the U.S. government's determination to lead the global aerospace market which is now focused on one national champion for civil transport aircraft," it added.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert made it abundantly clear in December, when the merger was announced, that conditions could be attached to the deal if it appeared likely to strengthen Boeing's already strong position in Europe.

The commission, the European Union's executive body, has the power to examine all corporate acquisitions or alliances involving companies with worldwide revenues of $5.754 billion and European revenues of $287 million each.
Airbus' partners are Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace, F, Aerospatiale of France, British Aerospace and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas.
